{{< include ../theme/_macros.qmd >}}

::: {.text-center .fs-2 .my-3 .text-primary}
Programs compose. Specifications compose.<br>
**Double categories let them compose [*together*]{.loose}.**
:::

::::::::: {.grid}

:::::: {.g-col-6}
::::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 1 · Two kinds of arrows

An ordinary category has one kind of arrow. A **double category** has two:

- [**tight arrows**]{.tight} are *programs*: things you **run**;
- [**loose arrows**]{.loose} are *specifications*: things you **check**;
- **squares** are evidence that the programs *respect* the specs.

::: {.imagify .big}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=7em, row sep=5em, sq={1-1}{2-2}]
  A \arrow[r, loose, "R"] \arrow[d, tight, "f"'] & B \arrow[d, tight, "g"] \\
  A' \arrow[r, loose, "R'"'] & B'
  \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2, phantom, "\Downarrow\alpha"]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

::: {.bg-strip .text-center .p-2 .rounded}
if $x \mathrel{\loose{R}} y$ then $\tight{f}(x) \mathrel{\loose{R'}} \tight{g}(y)$
:::

::::: {.example}
Take two *different* sorting algorithms, and the spec [perm]{.loose},
relating two lists that are rearrangements of each other.

::: {.imagify}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=6em, row sep=5em, sq={1-1}{2-2}]
  \mathsf{List\ Nat} \arrow[r, loose, "\mathsf{perm}"] \arrow[d, tight, "\mathsf{insertionSort}"'] &
  \mathsf{List\ Nat} \arrow[d, tight, "\mathsf{mergeSort}"] \\
  \mathsf{List\ Nat} \arrow[r, loose, "\mathsf{equal}"'] & \mathsf{List\ Nat}
  \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2, phantom, "\yes"]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

`insertionSort`{.tight} on `[3,1,2]` and `mergeSort`{.tight} on
`[2,3,1]` both give `[1,2,3]`. That holds for *every* pair of
permutations, so the square exists. The algorithms agree however
the input may be arranged.
:::::

::: {.experts}
A double category is a pseudo category object in
$\mathbf{Cat}$; loose composition is associative and unital only up to
coherent isomorphism [@grandis99].
:::
:::::

::::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 2 · You've met one: $\rel$

Objects are types, [tight arrows]{.tight} are functions, [loose
arrows]{.loose} are relations. A square means the functions
**preserve** the relation.

::::: {.example}
The relation $\loose{\mathsf{els}} : \mathsf{List\ Nat} \larr \mathsf{Set\ Nat}$
relates a list to the set of its elements.

:::: {.grid}
::: {.g-col-6}
::: {.imagify}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=5em, sq={1-1}{2-2}]
  \mathsf{List\ Nat} \arrow[r, loose, "\mathsf{els}"] \arrow[d, tight, "\mathsf{cons}\ x"'] &
  \mathsf{Set\ Nat} \arrow[d, tight, "\mathsf{insert}\ x"] \\
  \mathsf{List\ Nat} \arrow[r, loose, "\mathsf{els}"'] & \mathsf{Set\ Nat}
  \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2, phantom, "\yes"]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

If [els]{.loose} relates `xs` to `s`, it relates `cons x xs`{.tight}
to `insert x s`{.tight}, hence [cons]{.tight} implements [insert]{.tight}.
:::

::: {.g-col-6}
::: {.imagify}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=5em, nsq={1-1}{2-2}]
  \mathsf{List\ Nat} \arrow[r, loose, "\mathsf{els}"] \arrow[d, tight, "\mathsf{length}"'] &
  \mathsf{Set\ Nat} \arrow[d, tight, "\mathsf{size}"] \\
  \mathsf{Nat} \arrow[r, loose, "\mathsf{equal}"'] & \mathsf{Nat}
  \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2, phantom, "\no"]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

**Non-example.** [els]{.loose} relates `[1,1]` to `{1}`, but
`length`{.tight} gives 2 and `size`{.tight} gives 1. No square!
:::
::::
:::::

::: {.bg-strip .text-center .p-2 .rounded}
A square says *this implementation respects that abstraction*.
:::

::: {.experts}
This is data refinement; $\rel$ is an equipment, where
each function also gives a loose arrow, its graph [@shulman08].
:::
:::::
::::::

:::::: {.g-col-6}
::::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 3 · Squares are tiles

Squares glue like floor tiles, in two directions.

::: {.imagify}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=6em, row sep=4em, sq={1-1}{3-3}]
  \bullet \arrow[r, loose] \arrow[d, tight] &
  \bullet \arrow[r, loose] \arrow[d, tight] &
  \bullet \arrow[d, tight] \\
  \bullet \arrow[r, loose] \arrow[d, tight] &
  \bullet \arrow[r, loose] \arrow[d, tight] &
  \bullet \arrow[d, tight] \\
  \bullet \arrow[r, loose] &
  \bullet \arrow[r, loose] &
  \bullet
  \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2, phantom, "\alpha"]
  \arrow[from=1-2, to=2-3, phantom, "\beta"]
  \arrow[from=2-1, to=3-2, phantom, "\gamma"]
  \arrow[from=2-2, to=3-3, phantom, "\delta"]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

**Top to bottom, programs compose:** run one, then the next.

::: {.bg-strip .text-center .p-2 .rounded}
$(\tight{g} \circ \tight{f})(x) = \tight{g}(\tight{f}(x))$
:::

**Left to right, specs compose:** chain relations through a middle point.

::: {.bg-strip .text-center .p-2 .rounded}
$x \mathrel{(\loose{R} ; \loose{S})} z \iff \exists y.\ x \mathrel{\loose{R}} y \wedge y \mathrel{\loose{S}} z$
:::

Rows first or columns first gives **the same big square** (the
*interchange law*): the whole program meets the whole spec.

::: {.experts}
Squares with identity tight sides form a bicategory of
loose arrows; when every function also has a loose companion, the
double category is an *equipment* [@shulman08].
:::
:::::

::::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 4 · Trees and List Search

Binary search trees are optimised for search. There are many ways to represent a binary tree as a list, by tree traversal. This is gives another example of a square by having two different search algorithms one on trees and one on lists. The traversal is a true relation! 

Fixing a choice of key, a. 


::: {.imagify}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=8em, row sep=5em, sq={1-1}{2-2}]
  \mathsf{Tree}\ A \arrow[r, loose, "traversal"] \arrow[d, tight, "ListFind(a)"'] &
  \mathsf{List}\ A \arrow[d, tight, "TreeFind(a)"] \\
  \mathsf{Bool} \arrow[r, loose, "equal"'] & \mathsf{Bool}
  \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2, phantom, "\Downarrow \phi"]
\end{tikzcd}
:::

Both programs fail or succeed together however, depending on the model of computation, you may wish to ask how times a recursive call has been made. In this example then a square is not only describing that the programs compute the same way but carry extra data about those computations.


::: {.example}
Tree :

::: {.imagify}
\begin{tikzcd}
	& {} &&& \\
	& {(1)} \\
	{(2)} &&& {(3)} \\
	&& {(4)} && {(5)}
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=3-4]
	\arrow[from=3-4, to=4-3]
	\arrow[from=3-4, to=4-5]
\end{tikzcd}
:::


List obtained from in order traversal i.e. left-root-right traversal:

$$
[2, 1, 4, 3, 5]
$$
:::

::: {.experts}

:::
:::::

::::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 5 · Where they show up

- **Effects.** types, [terms]{.tight} and [effectful programs]{.loose}
  (state, exceptions, I/O).
- **Gradual Typing.** Types, [terms]{.tight}  and [type precision, $A \sqsubseteq B$]{.loose} 
- **Open systems.** Circuits, Petri nets, reaction networks:
  [maps of interfaces]{.tight} and [systems with boundaries]{.loose}.
- **Concurrency.** Machines, [homormorphisms]{.tight}, [bisimulation]{.loose}. 
- **Proof Relevant Relations.** Sets, [functions]{.tight} and [proof relevant relations]{.loose}
- **Distributors.** Groupoids, [functors]{.tight} and [distributors]{.loose}
- **Category theory.** Categories, [functors]{.tight} and [profunctors]{.loose}.
- **Topology.** Manifolds, [diffeomorphisms]{.tight} and [cobordisms]{.loose}.

::: {.experts}
Double categories go back to Ehresmann [@ehresmann63]. Effectful
programs form premonoidal categories and promonads [@power97;
@roman22; @jacobs2009categorical]; a more elementary definition is given by proof-irrelevant double categories or preorder categories [@new2020call]; distributors form a static model for linear logic [@clairambault2025thin
]; for those who are coalgebra minded [@hermida1998structural];
open systems form double categories of structured cospans
[@baez20].
:::

A double category is a category of [programs]{.tight} and a category of
[specifications]{.loose}, glued together by squares that say *"this
program meets this spec"*.
